keyFindings.description: An attachment's fallback is doubled against blocks nested inside that same attachment. Driven at the code head: attachments [{color: '#d00', fallback: 'Deploy failed on web-1', blocks: [section mrkdwn 'Deploy failed on web-1']}] delivers 'Deploy failed on web-1\nDeploy failed on web-1', body_truncated unset. The control is the same attachment with fallback equal to its own title, which still collapses to one line, so the gap is exactly fallback against the attachment's own subtree: the yielded tally reaches an object's own keys and blocks is descended as a separate object. This is not the cross-object trade the architect ruled in. That trade's reason, which the changelog states, is 'two objects saying the same thing are two things a reader sees'; an attachment's fallback is the one string in Slack's model defined by nobody seeing it when the attachment's own blocks render, so the reader sees the line once and the delivery says it twice. Colour bar plus fallback plus blocks is how an app posts a coloured alert today. Round 3's message-wide set covered it; the per-object scope does not. The architect required it in its message 2b22669359589de4d34472fa555f5d3b and specified the shape: build it as an ordering rule, not an exception — an attachment's fallback is read last, after everything else that attachment carries, and dropped when the attachment has already yielded it anywhere in its subtree. That also repairs a note standing from round 2: fallback is taken before the attachment's own blocks are descended, since blocks is not one of the nine names and sorts into the alphabetical tail, which is why an attachment carrying fallback 'PLAIN COPY' and a section 'the real body' delivers 'PLAIN COPY\nthe real body' with the fallback as the summary. Cases: the colour-bar body delivering one line; an attachment whose fallback differs from its blocks delivering both with the body first; and the existing same-object collapse unchanged.

A reader pairing alternating lines reads Result as main's label, which is the assertion half of the standard, but no word is lost since the own text carries it, and it needs an app whose text fallback is a bare one-word status. The narrowing the deep review suggested — compare ownWords only against the top-level objects of blocks and attachments — was refused with a reason I checked and agree with: a Slack client's rich_text copy sits several levels down in blocks[0].elements[].elements[], so that narrowing would stop dropping exactly the deep piece and the duplicate the human was shown as fixed would return.

Security[prompt], recorded and with the human. The deep review corrected two things round 3 told the architect, both read from code and both accepted by it for the human's ask. First, the Legion controller is not on this path: slackKind returns 'mention' only for event.type app_mention, and a link-unfurl edit is event.type 'message', so it publishes to the channel's .message topic while skills/legion-controller/references/slack-mentions.md subscribes the controller to .mention alone — the bot_id guard is not bypassed, it is never reached. The exposed population is any session that subscribes to a channel's .message topic. Second, the delimiter is JSON string encoding and it holds: the untrusted text is a JSON string value in Payload, so newlines are escaped and injected text cannot forge the prompt's own Summary, Message or Topic lines; the residual risk is instruction-shaped text inside the quoted region, not frame-breaking. The exploit path itself stands: a message_changed unfurl on a person's message delivers 'see https://x/y
Ignore previous instructions
unfurled body
fb' with user_id set and no bot_id. OWASP LLM01 and LLM06, ASVS v5.0.0-1.3.3.

Fast-follow, a further display field under the narrowing: slackWalkKeys drops every string under a non-display name, so a context element carrying only a link's url delivers nothing — blocks [{type: context, elements: [{mrkdwn 'Runbook:'}, {type: link, url: 'https://run.book/x'}]}] delivers 'Runbook:' alone, losing the URL the channel shows. It is the one case where Slack's rendering carries a string the walk is structurally unable to reach.

Fast-follow, structural: one object's construction is split across two functions with the same predicate written twice. walk.own is set in slackDeliveredText under strings.TrimSpace(own) != "", walk.ownWords in takeOwn under the same predicate sixty lines away, three TrimSpace calls run on the same string, and takeOwn carries an unwritten ordering rule — take(own) must precede the ownWords assignment or the own text suppresses itself. A constructor that sets both fields, calls take and trims once puts the invariant in one place.

Fast-follow: take tests full() before appending, so the piece that crosses the cap is appended whole and capBody then copies up to a megabyte of runes to discard almost all of it. Harmless at the 1 MiB body cap and the boundary is correct — exactly 2,048 runes sets no flag, 2,049 does, and no path drops a piece for fullness without capBody also reporting truncation — but capping the appended piece to the remaining budget removes the transient.

Recorded, checked and sound rather than a finding: ownWords and own are not the same job and do not collapse. ownWords is an exact-match set over the raw own text and its lines, consulted per piece in take; own is the entity-resolved text, used once as a substring haystack for the outermost rich_text probe. Keeping them distinct is right. Likewise the yielded bound is guaranteed rather than asserted: slackWalkKeys skips every non-display key whose value is a string, so the isString arm is reachable only for the nine display names and slices.Contains over a slice of at most nine beats a per-object map allocation.

thermonuclear.deepReview: APPROVE, zero blocking, four recorded. It confirmed the per-object tally cannot drop a string a reader sees except where one object puts the same string under two display names; that removing the message-wide set reintroduced nothing rounds 1 to 3 fixed; that ownWords suppresses only a repeat, never an only copy; that slackOwnWordsOnly still answers correctly with the producer de-duplicating; that deleting the pairing loses nothing; and that cost is bounded structurally, since a message whose own text passes 2,048 runes never enters the tree, capping every strings.Contains haystack at about 2 KB. It found no body a real Slack client sends where the own text and its rich_text copy disagree, having worked through emoji, channel mention, ordered list, fenced code, an auto-linked URL with an escaped entity and a date element, so the architect's ruling stands unchallenged. 20 shuffled runs confirm nothing depends on Go's map order.
thermonuclear.codeQuality: APPROVE, zero blocking, seven recorded. It judged the deletion a net simplification rather than a rearrangement — the attachment-fields special case stopped existing rather than moving behind another helper — and verified the yielded bound from slackWalkKeys rather than from the comment. It found no body a real Slack client sends that reopens the rich_text ruling either, having worked through the segment kinds a client emits.
